scenes.tts: A parent can gain a scar. Why is a baby not born with that scar? Follow the gold mark on this skin. Then follow the blue gene cards toward a young animal.
scenes.caption: A parent can gain a scar. Why is a baby not born with that scar? Follow the gold mark on this skin. Then follow the blue gene cards toward a young animal.
scenes.visual: COLOR MAP used throughout both films: genes and alleles blue; environment green; acquired body changes gold; routes to offspring teal; stopped routes red; other structures grey. Hook first on a dark field. A large grey parent mouse fills the left half. A gold scar grows across its skin while blue gene cards drift inside. At right, an unmarked young mouse waits behind a large question mark. The scar gently pulses and the gene cards stream toward the question mark.
scenes.narration: A parent can gain a scar. Why is a baby not born with that scar? Follow the gold mark on this skin. Then follow the blue gene cards toward a young animal.

scenes.visual: Brief title card after the hook: What Can Cross a Generation? Keep the parent, young mouse, gold scar, and drifting blue cards faintly visible behind the title.

scenes.tts: An inherited trait passes from parent to offspring through genes. An acquired trait develops during life. Eye color is inherited. A scar, dyed hair, a learned skill, and exercise-built muscle are acquired. These labels describe where the characteristic comes from, not whether genes act alone.
scenes.caption: An inherited trait passes from parent to offspring through genes. An acquired trait develops during life. Eye color is inherited. A scar, dyed hair, a learned skill, and exercise-built muscle are acquired. These labels describe where the characteristic comes from, not whether genes act alone.
scenes.visual: Transform the question mark into two wide paths leaving the same parent. The upper teal path begins at the blue gene cards and is labelled inherited. The lower gold path stays within the parent's body and is labelled acquired. Small cartoons transform in place: an eye beside the upper path; scar, dyed hair, piano keys, and a flexing muscle beside the lower path. Limit labels to inherited and acquired.
scenes.narration: An inherited trait passes from parent to offspring through genes. An acquired trait develops during life. Eye color is inherited. A scar, dyed hair, a learned skill, and exercise-built muscle are acquired. These labels describe where the characteristic comes from, not whether genes act alone.

scenes.tts: In people, mice, and many other animals, offspring begin from sex cells. Those cells carry the parents' genes. Skin cells can heal into a scar. Muscle cells can grow with exercise. Those body-cell changes do not change the genes inside the sex cells.
scenes.caption: In people, mice, and many other animals, offspring begin from sex cells. Those cells carry the parents' genes. Skin cells can heal into a scar. Muscle cells can grow with exercise. Those body-cell changes do not change the genes inside the sex cells.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the same parent. Show three large labelled regions: skin cells at the gold scar, muscle cells beside a growing gold muscle, and sex cells containing blue gene cards. Teal arrows extend only from the sex cells toward the young mouse. Gold ripples spread within skin and muscle but never cross into the sex-cell region.
scenes.narration: In people, mice, and many other animals, offspring begin from sex cells. Those cells carry the parents' genes. Skin cells can heal into a scar. Muscle cells can grow with exercise. Those body-cell changes do not change the genes inside the sex cells.

scenes.tts: The skin change and the gene cards now sit beside different paths. Which path can reach the offspring? Keep watching both routes before you decide.
scenes.caption: The skin change and the gene cards now sit beside different paths. Which path can reach the offspring? Keep watching both routes before you decide.
scenes.visual: Hold the large cell map. A gold scar icon and a blue gene card each approach separate gates leading toward the young mouse. Both gates remain neutral grey. Put the question Which path reaches the young? above them. Slow drifting motion continues in both icons.
scenes.narration: The skin change and the gene cards now sit beside different paths. Which path can reach the offspring? Keep watching both routes before you decide.

scenes.visual: Thinking pause. Keep the question visible. The gold scar icon and blue gene card slowly bob beside their neutral gates. Do not reveal either route yet.

scenes.tts: The blue cards pass through the sex-cell gate and continue into the young. The scar reaches a red stop at the body-cell gate. Gene-coded traits can pass on; ordinary changes gained during life cannot. Ordinary means body changes like the ones shown here.
scenes.caption: The blue cards pass through the sex-cell gate and continue into the young. The scar reaches a red stop at the body-cell gate. Gene-coded traits can pass on; ordinary changes gained during life cannot. Ordinary means body changes like the ones shown here.
scenes.visual: Open the sex-cell gate in teal. Animate blue cards through it into the young mouse, where matching blue cards settle. Turn the body-cell gate red and gently stop the gold scar icon there. Show the guiding rule once below the moving routes, then fade the sentence while the map remains.
scenes.narration: The blue cards pass through the sex-cell gate and continue into the young. The scar reaches a red stop at the body-cell gate. Gene-coded traits can pass on; ordinary changes gained during life cannot. Ordinary means body changes like the ones shown here.

scenes.tts: Genes are not the whole story. The environment is everything around a living thing that can affect it. Soil, light, water, food, and temperature belong to it. Genes and environment can work together to shape the phenotype, the trait that appears.
scenes.caption: Genes are not the whole story. The environment is everything around a living thing that can affect it. Soil, light, water, food, and temperature belong to it. Genes and environment can work together to shape the phenotype, the trait that appears.
scenes.visual: Transform the mouse map into a large plant cutting while keeping its blue gene cards in the same screen position. Build a green environment ring around it. Soil rises from below; light sweeps across; water droplets, a food icon, and a temperature gauge orbit slowly. The flower at top remains neutral while green conditions move. Label phenotype beside the flower.
scenes.narration: Genes are not the whole story. The environment is everything around a living thing that can affect it. Soil, light, water, food, and temperature belong to it. Genes and environment can work together to shape the phenotype, the trait that appears.

scenes.tts: Variation means differences among living things of the same kind. Some differences trace to inherited alleles. Others develop as environments differ. Many traits reflect both. Matching gene sets can meet different surroundings and produce different visible results. That is why tracing a cause works better than forcing every phenotype into a genes-only box or an environment-only box.
scenes.caption: Variation means differences among living things of the same kind. Some differences trace to inherited alleles. Others develop as environments differ. Many traits reflect both. Matching gene sets can meet different surroundings and produce different visible results. That is why tracing a cause works better than forcing every phenotype into a genes-only box or an environment-only box.
scenes.visual: Keep the carried plant central and grow several nearby plants from it. Vary blue allele cards in some plants and green environment rings around others. Let flower height and color shift gradually. Then slide away two large boxes labelled genes only and environment only. Replace them with overlapping blue and green circles behind the plants. Mark the flower differences schematic.
scenes.narration: Variation means differences among living things of the same kind. Some differences trace to inherited alleles. Others develop as environments differ. Many traits reflect both. Matching gene sets can meet different surroundings and produce different visible results. That is why tracing a cause works better than forcing every phenotype into a genes-only box or an environment-only box.

scenes.tts: Watch matching cuttings from a bigleaf hydrangea. Their blue gene cards stay the same. In many kinds, acidic soil lets roots take up more aluminum. That helps flowers become blue. Less acidic soil can give pink flowers. The soil changes the phenotype, not the cutting's genes.
scenes.caption: Watch matching cuttings from a bigleaf hydrangea. Their blue gene cards stay the same. In many kinds, acidic soil lets roots take up more aluminum. That helps flowers become blue. Less acidic soil can give pink flowers. The soil changes the phenotype, not the cutting's genes.
scenes.visual: Split the carried plant into matching cuttings with identical blue gene cards. Green soil beneath the left cutting becomes acidic; labelled aluminum dots move through its roots and its schematic flower gradually turns blue. The right soil becomes less acidic and its schematic flower gradually turns pink. Keep a small always-visible label: color response is schematic. Never change the blue gene cards.
scenes.narration: Watch matching cuttings from a bigleaf hydrangea. Their blue gene cards stay the same. In many kinds, acidic soil lets roots take up more aluminum. That helps flowers become blue. Less acidic soil can give pink flowers. The soil changes the phenotype, not the cutting's genes.

scenes.tts: Genes set which colors are possible, while soil helps decide which appears. The same logic explains why matching genes need not make matching phenotypes. Phenotype tells what appears, not which cause acted. First trace the cause. Then ask whether it can enter the gene route to offspring.

Phenotype tells what appears, not which cause acted. First trace the cause. Then ask whether it can enter the gene route to offspring.
scenes.visual: Show a short row of schematic possible flower colors above the gene cards, with the soil arrow pointing to which one appears. Do not show any white or always-pink variety; the lesson asks students to predict that. Return the main matching cuttings to center. A teal route leads from their unchanged blue gene cards toward seed offspring, while green soil arrows end at the flowers. Finish on the two distinct routes without a recap list.

Phenotype tells what appears, not which cause acted. First trace the cause. Then ask whether it can enter the gene route to offspring.

scenes.visual: End card. Show one line only: 'Gene-coded traits can pass on; ordinary changes gained during life cannot.'
